assertion.description: Rickettsia rickettsii is carried by Dermacentor and Rhipicephalus ticks, which are both its vectors and part of its maintenance: an infected female passes the agent transovarially to a high proportion of her offspring. Transovarial passage alone does not settle the question of maintenance, because the agent is lethal to the majority of infected ticks, which is offered as the reason infected ticks are scarce in the field. Vertebrate animals sustain the tick populations - immature ticks feed on rodents and rabbits, adults on larger mammals, and domestic dogs are the preferred host of the brown dog tick at every stage. Humans are incidental hosts.

The virus is passed in both vertical and horizontal transmission cycles within the tick population, and amplifying hosts spread virus from infected to uninfected ticks by co-feeding or by supporting a viraemic blood meal. Humans are incidental, dead-end hosts that do not maintain the cycle.

Humans enter it accidentally in the intermediate host position, where the cyst forms but the cycle stops.

There is no arthropod vector.

assertion.description: Yersinia pestis persists in enzootic sylvatic cycles between burrowing rodents and their fleas, with mice, rats, prairie dogs and ground squirrels among the hosts of established foci. Periodic epizootics kill off rodent colonies, which raises human exposure. The flea acquires the bacterium in a bloodmeal, a biofilm forms in the proventriculus, and a blocked flea regurgitates bacteria into the next bite wound; blockage is most frequent in the rat flea Xenopsylla cheopis. Humans are accidental hosts. Which small rodents, if any, sustain the agent between epizootics is unsettled.

assertion.description: Toxoplasma gondii completes sexual reproduction only in the intestinal epithelium of felids (the definitive hosts) and reproduces asexually in warm-blooded intermediate hosts, including humans. The human-relevant phases are the rapidly dividing tachyzoite of acute infection and the encysted bradyzoite of lifelong chronic infection.

hosts.role: Intermediate host supporting asexual replication and tissue-cyst formation

life_cycle_stages.name: Sexual replication in the feline intestinal epithelium
life_cycle_stages.description: Sexual reproduction is restricted to the gut epithelium of cats and other felids, which are therefore the only definitive hosts and the only source of environmental oocysts.

life_cycle_stages.name: Environmental oocyst stage shed in felid faeces
life_cycle_stages.description: Oocysts shed in cat faeces contaminate water, soil and crops and are the environmental infectious stage for intermediate hosts including humans.

life_cycle_stages.name: Asexual tachyzoite stage in intermediate hosts
life_cycle_stages.description: Ingested oocysts or bradyzoites invade the intestinal epithelium and transform into tachyzoites, the rapidly proliferating stage responsible for acute infection and dissemination.

life_cycle_stages.name: Chronic bradyzoite stage within tissue cysts
life_cycle_stages.description: Tachyzoites differentiate into bradyzoites that form intracellular tissue cysts, the latent stage that resists immune clearance and current drugs.

selected_evidence.snippet: The life cycle of T. gondii is composed of two reproductive stages: sexual and asexual stages in definitive and intermediate hosts, respectively.
